extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics, philosophers of science, and mathematicians interested in explanation and foundations
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply philosophical and practice-based criteria for when mathematical proofs, generalizations, or theories count as explanations (vs merely convincing derivations). Focuses on accounts by Steiner, Kitcher, and related discussions of generalization, unification, and indispensability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstraction and generalization as routes to satisfactory explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: “Abstraction and generalization are constantly pursued as the means to reach really satisfactory explanations which account for scattered individual results.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feferman-style rationale: extensive developments (e.g., in algebra and analysis) are often necessary to give real insight into behavior of simpler objects (e.g., natural numbers). Explanatory practice may legitimately appeal to more abstract entities (ideals, analytic functions) even when instances are finitistically checkable only; these abstract detours can provide the kind of insight lacking in purely finitary derivations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indispensability-style justificatory argument (Feferman reconstruction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three-step structure: (1) scattered results (data) call for explanation; (2) explanation is obtained by appealing to more abstract entities; (3) we have good reason to postulate and believe in those abstract entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a rational ground for accepting mathematical entities: if abstract apparatus yields explanatory power for earlier scattered results, that supports belief in those entities. Intended audience are mathematical realists not already committed to restrictive foundational positions (e.g., predicativism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory power trumps mere eliminability (explanatory conservativity concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: A derivation may be formally reducible to a narrower framework (conservative extension), but if that reduction entails a loss of explanatory power, we still have reason to believe in the original entities/methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raises the question: when is a derivation explanatory? Formal derivability alone does not guarantee explanatory adequacy; one must assess loss/gain of explanatory resources in translation/elimination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejecting causal-only demand for explanations (anti-causalist point)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dummett’s rejection of certain abstract entities relies on the questionable assumption that all explanations must be causal; mathematical explanations need not be causal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: dismissing mathematical explanatory appeal to abstract objects on grounds that they 'do not act' fails if one allows non-causal forms of explanation (typical in mathematics and formal sciences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner’s dependence-on-characterizing-property criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “An explanatory proof makes reference to a characterizing property of an entity or structure mentioned in the theorem, such that from the proof it is evident that the result depends on the property.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizing property = property unique to a given entity/structure within a family/domain. Explanatory proofs show dependence of the theorem on such a property, thereby elucidating why the result holds for that kind of structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steiner’s generalizability criterion (via deformations)
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory proof is generalizable: varying the relevant (characterizing) feature in such a proof gives rise to an array of corresponding theorems, proved—and explained—by an array of 'deformations' of the original proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steiner requires that explanatory proofs support systematic generalizations when the key feature is varied; explanatory power is evidenced by a proof family's ability to generate related theorems under controlled variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of simple heuristics (abstractness, visualizability, genetic aspects) as sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Steiner rejects initially plausible criteria for explanation such as (greater degree of) abstractness or generality of a proof, its visualizability, and its genetic aspect as adequate markers of explanatoriness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating mere abstractness, generality, visualizability, or the fact that a proof mirrors discovery heuristics as sufficient for explanation. These can be neither necessary nor sufficient without further structure (e.g., characterizing properties, generalizability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory vs. non-explanatory proofs distinguished by practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians often find proofs convincing yet unsatisfactory if they 'throw no light on the why and wherefore' of the procedure; explanatoriness is a practice-sensitive notion (Mordell's phenomenon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for explanatory adequacy should account for practitioners' judgments: a proof that leaves mathematicians feeling 'something is missing' is non-explanatory even if logically valid. Case studies (e.g., Kummer's criterion) provide empirical data for theorizing explanatoriness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fruitful (explanatory) vs. sterile (non-explanatory) generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Fruitful generalizations reveal in a single principle the rationale of many particular truths and thereby are explanatory; sterile generalizations merely extend to unimportant cases without improving explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Cournot and Mandelbrojt: measure a generalization by its capacity to reveal explanatory order or to put objects in a 'natural setting'. Cheap/sterile generalizations are anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kitcher’s unification criterion: minimize argument-patterns while maximizing conclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding increases by reducing the number of independent phenomena/argument patterns; the explanatory store E(K) is the systematization that best trades off minimizing distinct derivation patterns and maximizing the number of conclusions generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalize explanation as selection of a best systematization (E(K)): prefer derivational patterns that reoccur across many cases. Explanations are derivations (sequences showing how premises yield conclusions), and the global best systematization confers explanatoriness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation as global/systematization property (derivations, not local arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatoriness is not a purely local property of isolated premise–conclusion pairs; rather, an argument counts as explanatory insofar as it belongs to a best systematization of beliefs (E(K)). Arguments should be assessed as derivations (sequence with specified rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: treating single premise–conclusion pairs as fully evaluable for explanatoriness without regard for their role in the broader systematization. Prioritize derivational structure and contribution to unified explanatory patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of generality-as-complexity criterion (induction example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Kitcher objects to measuring generality by logical complexity (e.g., claiming proofs are explanatory iff premises are at least as general as conclusion), using induction to show arithmetic proofs can be explanatory despite apparent violations of that generality measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate formula-level logical generality with explanatory relevance; reformulations and the structure of derivations (e.g., induction reformulated as single universal premise) show that simplistic syntactic measures of generality are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant generalizations must illuminate developed areas to be rationally acceptable
rubrics_metrics.description: Those 'generalizing' stipulations which fail to illuminate those areas of mathematics which have already been developed are not rationally acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kitcher: judge proposed generalizations by their capacity to make sense of existing theory (show old theory as special case of a family). Generalizations that do not increase explanatory understanding of prior results are to be rejected as trivial or irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatoriness can be a property of theory/framework as well as individual proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Some explanations arise from major conceptual recastings of a discipline, where explanatoriness is primarily a property of the whole theory or framework and proofs are explanatory by virtue of belonging to that framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish two levels: (a) explanatoriness as a property of individual proofs (Steiner-style); (b) holistic explanatoriness where reconceptualization of a theory provides explanatory insight and subsequent proofs derive explanatoriness from the framework (cases from complex analysis).
